title: Fish Oil Supplements Don't Protect Your Brain From Alzheimer's, a Rigorous Two-Year Trial Confirms
excerpt: A USC Keck School of Medicine study found that high-dose omega-3 reached the brain but failed to improve memory, prevent cell loss, or slow cognitive decline — upending the $1 billion supplement industry's core claim.
body:
Americans spend more than $1 billion a year on fish oil supplements, making omega-3 capsules the single most popular supplement in the country after multivitamins. The pitch is hard to resist: take a daily pill, protect your heart, sharpen your brain, maybe even stave off dementia. But a rigorous new clinical trial has just delivered an uncomfortable verdict for anyone banking on that promise.

A two-year, placebo-controlled, double-blind study from the Keck School of Medicine at the University of Southern California — published in *eBioMedicine*, a Lancet journal — found that high-dose omega-3 supplements had no measurable impact on brain health in adults at elevated risk of Alzheimer's disease. No improvement in memory. No improvement in cognitive function. No reduction in the brain cell loss that is Alzheimer's hallmark.

"We all wish there was a silver bullet for preventing Alzheimer's, but our findings showed that fish oil supplements do not appear to protect brain health," said Dr. Hussein Naji Yassine, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health and lead investigator of the study.

## The Study: Omega-3 Reached the Brain — and Still Did Nothing

What makes this trial particularly significant is that the researchers didn't just test whether supplements helped. They first confirmed that the omega-3 was actually getting to where it needed to go.

The team recruited 365 adults between the ages of 55 and 80 who rarely ate fish and were considered at elevated risk for Alzheimer's. Nearly half — 47 percent — carried the APOE4 gene, the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 2,000 mg of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) daily or a placebo.

After six months, researchers measured DHA levels in cerebrospinal fluid — the fluid surrounding the brain — and found a 17 percent increase, confirming the supplement was reaching the central nervous system. But when they tested memory and cognitive abilities at baseline and again two years later, the DHA group performed no better than the placebo group. Brain scans showed no difference in hippocampal shrinkage, the brain region most closely associated with memory and Alzheimer's progression.

"Our study shows that high-dose DHA can reach the brain, but supplementation alone still did not improve cognition or brain imaging outcomes," Yassine told *Inc.* "That suggests the issue is not simply dose or delivery."

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

The finding carries particular weight for South Asian communities. Multiple studies — including the landmark MASALA study from Northwestern University — have shown that South Asians face disproportionately high rates of cardiovascular disease, Type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, all of which are independent risk factors for Alzheimer's. A 2024 Lancet Commission report estimated that up to 40 percent of dementia cases are attributable to modifiable risk factors, many of which cluster more heavily in South Asian populations.

Fish oil supplements are widely used across the Indian diaspora — often recommended by family members or Ayurvedic practitioners as a general brain and heart tonic. This study suggests that relying on supplements alone, without addressing underlying metabolic health, dietary patterns, and lifestyle factors, is unlikely to provide the protection many assume.

## The Mediterranean Diet May Hold the Key

Yassine's team is now investigating why omega-3s in whole foods appear to have a different effect than the same molecules in pill form. Their working hypothesis: omega-3 fatty acids may work best as part of a Mediterranean-style diet — rich in fish, olive oil, nuts, vegetables, and whole grains — rather than as an isolated supplement.

"We're focused on better understanding how the brain processes omega-3s and whether factors such as poor health, dietary pattern, genetic risk and age may change the brain's ability to effectively absorb and use omega-3s," Yassine said.

The Mediterranean diet has been consistently associated with lower Alzheimer's risk in observational studies. A traditional South Indian diet — heavy on coconut, fish, leafy greens, turmeric, and lentils — shares several of these protective characteristics, but the processed Western diet adopted by many NRIs does not.

## The Bigger Picture

The study does not argue that omega-3 fatty acids are useless. They remain essential nutrients that play a vital role in forming brain cell connections. What the evidence now shows is that popping fish oil capsules is not the shortcut to brain protection that the supplement industry has been selling.

"Staying healthy throughout life remains the most powerful tool we have for reducing Alzheimer's risk, including regular exercise, quality sleep and a balanced diet," Yassine said. "Living a healthy lifestyle is the brain's equivalent of getting regular car maintenance."

For NRIs managing the unique metabolic risks that come with South Asian genetics — higher visceral fat, insulin resistance, earlier cardiovascular events — the message is clear: supplements are not a substitute for the hard, daily work of eating well, moving regularly, sleeping enough, and managing blood sugar and blood pressure before they cause irreversible damage.

*Sources: eBioMedicine (The Lancet), USC Keck School of Medicine, Medicalxpress, Inc.*
